blocks.text: Raised intracranial pressure occurs when the pressure within the cranial cavity increases beyond normal levels.
Normal adult ICP is approximately 5–15 mmHg. Sustained ICP above 20–22 mmHg is generally concerning in severe traumatic brain injury.

rows: Intracranial haemorrhage, subdural haematoma, epidural haematoma
Stroke, cerebral infarction, traumatic brain injury

blocks.title: The skull is a rigid compartment containing three major components:

blocks.text: An increase in one component must initially be compensated for by a reduction in another. Once compensatory mechanisms are exhausted, ICP rises rapidly.
Late sign
Cushing's triad suggests severe raised ICP and possible impending brainstem compression.
Papilloedema is optic disc swelling caused by raised intracranial pressure.
Mnemonic: HEAD

items.text: H – Head elevation approximately 30°, keeping the neck neutral.
E – Ensure oxygenation and adequate ventilation.
A – Avoid hypotension and maintain cerebral perfusion.
D – Decompress or treat the underlying cause.
Hypertonic saline or mannitol in appropriate patients.
External ventricular drainage in selected cases.
Surgical evacuation of mass lesions where indicated.

blocks.text: Clinical pearl: In a patient with suspected raised ICP, avoid lumbar puncture until an intracranial mass lesion or dangerous pressure gradient has been excluded.
Hydrocephalus is abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) within the ventricular system, usually resulting in ventricular enlargement.

rows: Widened CSF pathways due to developmental or structural abnormalities

blocks.text: 1. Communicating hydrocephalus
CSF can pass through the ventricular system, but absorption is impaired or, rarely, production is excessive.
2. Non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus
There is an obstruction within the ventricular system.

items.text: Colloid cyst of the third ventricle.

items.text: Cranial ultrasound in infants with an open fontanelle.
CSF studies where appropriate and safe.
In suspected NPH, specialist assessment and CSF drainage testing may help predict response to shunting.
Endoscopic third ventriculostomy in selected obstructive cases.
Monitor for shunt obstruction, infection and overdrainage.

rows: Degenerative vascular disease, e.g. cerebral amyloid angiopathy

items.text: Haemorrhagic transformation of an ischaemic stroke.
Neck stiffness, especially in subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Unequal pupils or abnormal posturing in severe cases.

Manage blood pressure according to haemorrhage type and protocol.

blocks.text: Clinical pearl: Sudden thunderclap headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds to minutes should raise suspicion of subarachnoid haemorrhage.

Spinal cord compression occurs when a lesion or process compresses the spinal cord, causing neurological dysfunction.

rows: Narrowing of the spinal canal – spinal stenosis
Ligamentous disease, e.g. ossification of posterior longitudinal ligament

blocks.text: Mnemonic: CORD

items.text: D – Disturbed sensation and sphincter dysfunction.

blocks.text: Specific findings depend on the level:

rows: Weakness in all four limbs, sensory changes, possible respiratory compromise
Lower-limb weakness, sensory level and bladder dysfunction
Lower-limb neurological deficits; cauda equina syndrome if nerve roots are involved

content_groups.group_title: Upper versus lower motor neuron signs

items.text: Urgent MRI of the whole spine when metastatic spinal cord compression is suspected.
CT for bony anatomy and fractures.
Full blood count, ESR and CRP.
Blood cultures if infection is suspected.

blocks.text: Emergency

items.text: Immobilisation or spinal precautions where instability is suspected.
Corticosteroids, commonly dexamethasone, in suspected metastatic spinal cord compression with neurological signs, according to local protocol.
Decompression surgery and/or radiotherapy depending on cause.
Antibiotics and drainage for spinal epidural abscess.

blocks.text: Clinical pearl: New limb weakness, a sensory level or sphincter dysfunction in a patient with known cancer should be treated as metastatic spinal cord compression until excluded.
Cauda equina syndrome occurs when the lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus medullaris are compressed.

rows: Abnormal masses, including tumours and haematomas
Usually upper motor neuron features below lesion

items.text: Bladder scan for post-void residual volume.
Additional imaging if MRI is unavailable or contraindicated.

blocks.text: Do not miss
A normal rectal tone examination or a low post-void residual does not reliably exclude early cauda equina syndrome. Clinical suspicion requires urgent assessment.
Head injury is trauma to the scalp, skull or intracranial structures.

blocks.text: Primary injury: Occurs at the time of trauma.
Secondary injury: Develops after the initial trauma.

rows: Disability: GCS, pupils, glucose and limb movement
Exposure and examination for other injuries

items.text: Suspected open or depressed skull fracture.

Complications may be immediate, early or delayed.

rows: Infection, particularly with open injuries or CSF leaks

Medial temporal lobe displaced; may compress CN III

blocks.text: Uncal herniation: Classically causes ipsilateral dilated pupil due to compression of the third cranial nerve.

items.text: Post-traumatic epilepsy: recurrent unprovoked seizures after brain injury.

blocks.text: Mnemonic: PROTECT

items.text: O – Observe GCS and pupils regularly.
C – Control temperature and glucose abnormalities.
T – Treat associated injuries and complications.
